The majority voted in favour of [government amendments](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2018-09-11.4.2) (1) to (5) and (8) to (11), which means they succeeded. ### What do these amendments do? These amendments would move several matters that are currently in disallowable instruments - that is, legislative instruments that the parliament is able to vote against in a single vote so they stop being law - to standard legislation that can't so easily be undone. These matters include the location of the trial sites. According to Liberal MP [Mitch Fifield](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/victoria/mitch_fifield), who introduced the amendments, *"[this will give certainty](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2018-09-11.6.1) to trial participants and local communities"*. ### What does the bill do? The [bill was introduced to](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6130): * *expand the cashless debit card arrangements to a further trial site, the Bundaberg and Hervey Bay area, to run until 30 June 2020;* * *specify the class of trial participants for the area and increase the total number of trial participants overall to 15 000;* * *provide for an exception from the restrictive trade practices provisions of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 for merchants that implement product level blocking systems to identify that a cashless debit card is being used for payment and, if any restricted products are being purchased, decline the transaction; and* * *limit the use of the restricted portion of a payment to prevent the portion being used to obtain cash-like products which could be used to obtain alcohol or gambling.*
Social Services Legislation Amendment (Cashless Debit Card Trial Expansion) Bill 2018 - Third Reading - Pass the bill

Labor opposed the expansion of the cashless debit card trial to Bundaberg and Hervey Bay, citing community opposition from both local mayors, a lack of formal consultation, an inconclusive and poor-quality ORIMA evaluation, and program costs exceeding $24 million to date (including $7.9 million paid to Indue and $1.6 million to ORIMA). It committed to supporting the current trials in Ceduna and the East Kimberley until mid-2019, but would only consider new sites with credible evidence of effectiveness and an agreed community consultation process and definition of consent.

The speaker argued for the expansion of the Cashless Debit Card trial to the Hinkler electorate, citing strong community support, over 188 consultation meetings, a ReachTEL poll showing 27.8% opposition, and a cost of less than $2,000 per person. They invited the member for Barton to meet frontline service providers rather than union officials, and noted that the trial would affect 6,700 participants on specific welfare payments to address child neglect and gambling-related harm.

The speaker argued for expanding the Cashless Debit Card trial to Bundaberg and Hervey Bay, citing independent evaluation results showing reduced alcohol and drug use, gambling, and improved savings and childcare in existing trial sites (Ceduna and East Kimberley). The bill extends the trial to about 6,700 welfare recipients under 36 in those areas, with additional $1 million in community services, and amends the list of restricted goods to include cash-like products.

The member for Herbert opposed the cashless debit card trial expansion, arguing it should not be imposed on communities that reject it, and instead advocated for early intervention and prevention programs, citing a $5 million commitment to a Salvation Army detox facility and noting that 78% of trial participants reported little or no change.

The speaker opposed the bill to expand the cashless debit card trial to Bundaberg and Hervey Bay, arguing the government failed to properly consult communities and lacked credible evidence. They noted the expansion would add around 6,700 participants, bringing the total to over 15,000, and criticised the $1.6 million ORIMA evaluation as unreliable while highlighting the $24 million spent on existing trials.

The bill expands the cashless debit card trial to Bundaberg and Hervey Bay, covering around 6,700 people under 36 on Newstart, youth allowance, or parenting payments, running until 30 June 2020, based on community consultation and evidence of intergenerational welfare dependency.

The speaker argued against expanding the Cashless Debit Card trial to Bundaberg and Hervey Bay, citing a woeful evaluation, no reduction in violence, and a damning Auditor-General's report, while supporting continuation of existing trials in Ceduna and East Kimberley for two years. They opposed the national rollout, insisting on genuine community consultation and wraparound services instead of mandatory income management.

Labor opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, which would have drug-tested 5,000 Newstart and youth allowance recipients in Canterbury Bankstown, Logan, and Mandurah, citing no evidence of effectiveness, opposition from medical and community experts, potential to increase crime and homelessness, and high testing costs.

The speaker supported the government's drug-testing trial for 5,000 Newstart and youth allowance recipients in Canterbury Bankstown, Logan, and Mandurah, arguing it would identify and help welfare recipients with substance abuse through income management and treatment, with refusal resulting in loss of benefits.

The Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018 would drug test 5,000 Newstart and youth allowance recipients in three locations including Logan, Queensland, but lacks evidence and will harm vulnerable Australians, contrasting with an $80 billion tax handout to big business. No health or community organizations support the trial.

The speaker argued for the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, which would drug test 5,000 new Newstart and youth allowance recipients in Canterbury Bankstown, Logan, and Mandurah over two years, with a $10 million treatment fund to help those who test positive get clean and into work.

The Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, which would establish drug testing trials for welfare recipients in Canterbury Bankstown, Mandurah, and Logan City, was opposed as a punitive and evidence-free measure that would further marginalise vulnerable people, with no expert or community support and undisclosed costs.

The speaker argued that the Drug Testing Trial Bill 2018 should be passed, applying random drug tests to new Newstart and youth allowance recipients in Mandurah and two other trial sites, with positive results leading to income management and referral to treatment. They cited local support, a $10 million boost for drug treatment services, and existing government investments in Mandurah including $2 million for a youth health hub, $581 million for the Tonkin Highway extension, and a drop in unemployment from 11.6% to 6.5%.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, arguing it is arbitrary, cruel, and lacks evidence, and that drug addiction should be treated as a health issue rather than a punitive measure. They noted the trial would randomly test 5,000 Newstart and youth allowance recipients, with payment cancellation for refusal, and cited opposition from medical experts and community organisations, as well as long waits for rehabilitation.

The speaker argued in favour of the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, which would introduce drug testing for Newstart and youth allowance recipients in trial sites at Logan (Queensland), Mandurah (Western Australia) and Canterbury-Bankstown (New South Wales). The speaker stated the trial is not about punishment but about identifying and supporting people with drug dependencies through counselling, rehabilitation and a $10 million treatment fund, and noted that around 2,500 people would be tested over two years.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, arguing it would stigmatise jobseekers, lacked evidence, and was costly, with only 100 to 120 people expected to test positive a second time across the three trial sites in Canterbury Bankstown, Logan, and Mandurah.

The speaker argued for the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, a trial of 5,000 people in Canterbury-Bankstown, Logan, and Mandurah, where Newstart and youth allowance recipients would face drug testing, with first failure leading to 80% of income on a BasicsCard and second failure triggering referral to medical assessment and rehabilitation, funded by $10 million.

Labor opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, arguing it is based on flawed assumptions and would harm vulnerable people. The party cited evidence from medical and welfare experts, including 982 health professionals, that drug testing welfare recipients is ineffective and costly, with trials in New Zealand and the US returning very few positive results.

The speaker argued for the drug testing trial in the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, describing it as a non-punitive, world-leading measure to break intergenerational welfare dependency and drug addiction, citing 83% coalition voter support and 65% Labor voter support, and referencing the $685 million national ice initiative and $10 million for trial areas.

Centre Alliance maintained its opposition to the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, arguing it is a rebadged version of a previously rejected bill with no published costings, and citing US evidence that such programs are ineffective and expensive. The party called on parliament to again reject the legislation, stating that existing addiction services are underfunded and that the bill is a populist attempt to demonise welfare recipients.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, arguing it would drive up crime and demonise welfare recipients, citing the opposition of a former Australian Federal Police commissioner and the lack of any credible expert support.

The bill introduces a two-year drug testing trial for 5,000 new Newstart and youth allowance recipients in Canterbury Bankstown, Logan, and Mandurah, with income management for positive tests and a $10 million treatment fund. The speaker argued the trial identifies jobseekers with drug abuse issues and helps them access treatment and employment.
This bill would change how student loan debts are repaid and indexed to make the Higher Education Loan Program more sustainable.

It would set new repayment thresholds and rates for HELP loans from 1 July 2018, with a minimum threshold of $45,000 and a one per cent repayment rate, rising to a top threshold of $131,989 at ten per cent.

From 1 July 2019, HELP repayment thresholds would be indexed using the Consumer Price Index instead of Average Weekly Earnings, and from 2019–20, SFSS repayment thresholds would align with HELP thresholds.

The Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 was introduced to reduce regulatory burden by removing the five-voyage minimum for temporary licences, relaxing tolerance provisions, simplifying consultation requirements, and extending coverage to floating production storage and offloading units and dry-docking vessels. The bill aims to address the expected 30% growth in Australia's freight task by 2030, with coastal shipping currently projected to increase only 15%.

The 2012 Coastal Trading Act failed to halt the decline of Australian shipping, and the 2017 amendment bill should be passed to allow foreign superyachts to charter in Australia by removing customs import duties, which could create 11,800 jobs and $1.64 billion in economic benefit by 2021.

The speaker opposed the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it would allow foreign vessels to dominate Australian coastal trade, undermine Australian jobs and wages, and cited that the 2015 bill's regulatory impact statement predicted 1,000 of 1,100 maritime workers would be sacked. They highlighted opposition from the Maritime Union of Australia, Maritime Industry Australia Limited, and the Australian Institute of Marine and Power Engineers, and referenced the MV Portland and CSL Melbourne incidents where Australian crews were replaced by foreign crews.

The speaker argued that the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 would benefit their electorate of Fisher by boosting tourism and economic activity through relaxed superyacht regulations. They cited potential growth in GDP contributions from $590 million to $3.34 billion by 2021 and 8,100 additional jobs, with specific reference to the Mooloolaba Spit and Browns Slipway.

The Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 will decimate seafaring jobs and the maritime industry in Australia. The speaker waited 11 weeks through a gruelling by-election campaign to speak on this bill.

The bill would cause hundreds of Australian seafarer job losses, particularly in Tasmania, by allowing foreign ships and crews to replace Australian vessels on coastal routes, and was developed without consulting the peak shipping industry body, Maritime Industry Australia Ltd.

The speaker opposed the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it would accelerate the decline of Australia's merchant fleet and harm national security, environmental protection, and jobs—noting that 12 Australian-flagged vessels have been reflagged under the current government and that the bill's regulatory impact statement explicitly aims to remove barriers for foreign vessels.

The speaker argued that the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 should be passed to remove customs duties and taxes on superyachts, allow temporary licences for round trips, and enable charters, which would generate $1.64 billion and create nearly 12,000 jobs, particularly in Queensland regions like the Whitsundays, Bowen, and Cairns.

The speaker argued against the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017, accusing the Liberal Party of seeking to decimate Australian coastal shipping by replacing Australian vessels, workers, and wages with foreign ones. The majority voted to agree with [the bill's](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fbillhome%2Fr5816%22) main idea. This means that they can now discuss the bill in more detail. ### What is the bill's main idea? The bill was introduced to tighten the information disclosure requirements for the working holiday maker employer register. Firstly, it will ensure that details of the working holiday maker employer register will not be able to be made publicly available. Secondly, it'll ensure that information sharing between the Australian Tax Office (ATO) and the Fair Work Ombudsman (FWO) is only undertaken in situations in which an entity is non-compliant, or is reasonably suspected of non-compliance, with a tax law. Read more in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1617a/17bd088).

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2018-09-19.4.2) to agree with the bill's main idea. Farm Household Support Amendment (Temporary Measures) Bill 2018

The speaker announced the Farm Household Support Amendment (Temporary Measures) Bill 2018, which increases the farm assets threshold to a net $5 million until 30 June 2019 and pays a supplement of up to $12,000 per household to eligible Farm Household Allowance recipients. The speaker also urged farmers to call the Rural Financial Counselling Service on 1800686175 or the family assistance hotline on 132316, and noted that $5 million has been allocated for face-to-face counselling, while highlighting a request to supermarket CEOs for a 20-cent price increase on milk to support dairy farmers.
Treasury Laws Amendment (Medicare Levy and Medicare Levy Surcharge) Bill 2018

The speaker argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Medicare Levy and Medicare Levy Surcharge) Bill 2018 adjusts low-income thresholds in line with CPI to prevent low-income families from paying the Medicare levy, and highlighted record government investment in Medicare, hospitals, schools, disability services, and the PBS, including $34.4 billion added to the Medicare Guarantee Fund and $35.3 billion for MBS and PBS expenditure in 2018-19.
National Redress Scheme for Institutional Child Sexual Abuse Bill 2018

The speaker argued for the National Redress Scheme for Institutional Child Sexual Abuse Bill 2018, which will begin on 1 July and run for 10 years, offering monetary payments of up to $150,000 (average $76,000), counselling, and a direct personal response from participating institutions. New South Wales, Victoria and the Australian Capital Territory have already announced their participation, and the scheme could eventually provide redress to around 60,000 survivors if all states and institutions opt in.
Treasury Laws Amendment (Personal Income Tax Plan) Bill 2018

The Treasury Laws Amendment (Personal Income Tax Plan) Bill 2018 will provide immediate tax relief of up to $530 for low- and middle-income earners over four years, a $135 tax cut for three million people from July 2018, and eventually flatten the system so that 94% of taxpayers pay only 32.5 cents in the dollar. The plan aims to tackle bracket creep, reward hard work, and drive a stronger economy.
Treasury Laws Amendment (National Housing and Homelessness Agreement) Bill 2018

The speaker argued that the new Housing and Homelessness Agreement with tied funding is needed because previous funding of over $9 billion since 2009 failed to meet three of four benchmarks, with homelessness increasing 17.3% and rental stress rising 7%. The speaker also stated that domestic violence victims should not have to leave their homes; instead, state laws should remove perpetrators.
Treasury Laws Amendment (Banking Executive Accountability and Related Measures) Bill 2018

The speaker argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Banking Executive Accountability and Related Measures) Bill 2017 establishes a Banking Executive Accountability Regime (BEAR) to strengthen responsibility and accountability for senior banking executives and directors, giving APRA new powers to disqualify individuals and impose fines. The speaker also stated that the bill is not a result of the banking royal commission, which was only beginning, and criticised banks for prioritising shareholder interests over customers, citing evidence of manipulated loans and inadequate rescue options for smaller customers.
Medicare Levy Amendment (National Disability Insurance Scheme Funding) Bill 2017

The speaker argued for passing the Medicare Levy Amendment (NDIS Funding) Bill 2017, which would increase the Medicare levy by 0.5% to fund the National Disability Insurance Scheme. They named local disability champions including Brad Rossiter, Lauren Ball, Jackie Kay, Luke Stojanovic, and Brent Peter Kelly, and cited that the NDIS will support 460,000 Australians under 65 with permanent disability, with an estimated extra $3.4 billion in services needed.
